result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.eulerian_circuit()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find an Eulerian circuit in the graph if one exists. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L31920-L32018){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.eulerian_circuit() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Eulerian circuit](/assets/graphs/eulerian-circuit.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="Two triangles sharing node C, so every node has even degree. The Eulerian circuit starts and ends at C and uses each of the six edges exactly once; edges are numbered in the order the circuit takes them, and the card lists C, E, D, C, A, B, C." width="100%"} An Eulerian circuit is a closed trail that visits every edge exactly once, starting and ending at the same node. Uses Hierholzer's algorithm. Nodes may be (and usually are) visited several times; it is the edges that are each used exactly once. A circuit exists only when every node has even degree (undirected graphs) or equal in-degree and out-degree (directed graphs), and all nodes that have edges belong to one connected component (weakly connected, for directed graphs). If these conditions fail the method returns `None`, so it doubles as a test; `is_eulerian()` performs the same check without building the circuit. Eulerian circuits solve "cover every link once and come back" problems, such as: - route inspection: street sweeping, snow plowing, or mail delivery along every street - drawing a figure in one continuous stroke without retracing a line - sequencing problems that reduce to walking every edge of a graph (e.g. de Bruijn graphs in genome assembly) The circuit starts at an arbitrary node that has edges, and when several valid circuits exist only one is returned. Isolated nodes are ignored: they don't affect the existence check and never appear in the circuit. The method does not modify the graph. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Optional[list[int]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of node IDs forming the Eulerian circuit, or `None` if no circuit exists. The circuit starts and ends at the same node, so for a graph with `m` edges the list has `m + 1` entries. A graph with no nodes gives an empty list, and a single node with no edges gives a one-element list. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} An Eulerian circuit traverses every edge exactly once and returns to its starting node, and Hierholzer's algorithm (1873) constructs one in $O(E)$ time by repeatedly stitching sub-circuits together as soon as they close. The construction only works if one actually exists: every node must have even degree in the undirected case, or in-degree equal to out-degree in the directed case, and the graph must be connected on the vertices that carry edges (weak connectedness suffices in the directed setting). Call `is_eulerian()` first if that's not guaranteed, since this method simply returns `None` when the preconditions fail. Semi-Eulerian graphs (open Eulerian trail, no circuit) need a slightly different variant that starts at one of the two odd-degree nodes; `is_semieulerian()` tests for that case. The circuit returned here is one of possibly many valid ones. ## Examples {.doc-examples} On a cycle graph, the circuit simply goes once around the ring. Its length is one more than the number of edges, because the start node is repeated at the end: ::: {#e68ea39c .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_cycle_graph(5) graph.eulerian_circuit() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [3, 4, 5, 1, 2, 3] ``` ::: ::: Two triangles sharing node `C` form a "bowtie" in which every node has even degree. The circuit uses all six edges once and passes through the shared node `C` more than once: ::: {#1a4fd2e6 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D", "E"]) .add_edges([("A", "B"), ("B", "C"), ("C", "A"), ("C", "D"), ("D", "E"), ("E", "C")]) ) [graph.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in graph.eulerian_circuit()] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` ['C', 'E', 'D', 'C', 'A', 'B', 'C'] ``` ::: ::: A path graph has no Eulerian circuit: its two endpoints have odd degree, so there's no way to use every edge and return to the start. The method returns `None`: ::: {#62795d92 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_path_graph(5) graph.eulerian_circuit() is None ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` True ``` ::: ::: Directed graphs work the same way, as long as every node's in-degree equals its out-degree. A directed 5-cycle qualifies, and the circuit follows the edge directions: ::: {#e8359bcd .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph(directed=True) graph.add_cycle_graph(5) graph.eulerian_circuit() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` [3, 4, 5, 1, 2, 3] ``` ::: :::
